questions.question: Define urbanisation, urban growth, urban expansion and urban sprawl, making the separators between them clear.
questions.expected_answer: Urbanisation is the increasing percentage of a population living in urban areas — a proportion. Urban growth is the increase in the actual number of urban dwellers. Urban expansion is the physical outward spreading of the built-up area, while urban sprawl is low-density, unplanned or poorly planned outward spread that consumes farmland and forces long commutes — all sprawl is expansion, but planned compact growth expands without sprawling.

questions.question: Explain the functional classification of trade and transport towns, giving a South African example of each type.
questions.expected_answer: A break-of-bulk point is where cargo transfers between transport modes, attracting processing industry — Durban's port. A junction town grows where routes meet or cross — De Aar's railway junction. A gateway town controls entry between regions or countries — Musina at the Beitbridge border. A gap town commands a natural passage through a mountain barrier — Worcester or Ceres at passes through the Cape Fold Mountains.

questions.question: Describe the land-use zones of a South African city from the centre outwards, noting how apartheid planning altered the residential pattern.
questions.expected_answer: The CBD has the highest land values, tallest buildings and greatest accessibility, busy by day and empty at night. Around it lies the transition zone of mixed, changing land use — subdivided old buildings, light industry, decay and renewal. Beyond are residential zones sorted by income, but apartheid placed townships like Soweto and Khayelitsha on the far urban edge behind buffer strips, railways and industrial land, giving low-income residents the longest commutes. Heavy industry follows railways, highways and harbours; decentralised nodes like Sandton pull CBD functions to the suburbs, contributing to CBD decline and renewal efforts.
